Geometric Perspective: Approximation and Distance in Function Spaces

When we cannot take an infinite number of terms in actual calculations, we can only truncate it to a finite sum of the first terms, , to approximate the original function . So, how do we measure the “quality of approximation”? This prompts us to establish the geometry of function spaces, i.e., to define a “distance” (norm).

There are two different philosophies of “measurement of error” here:

1. Uniform Norm ( norm) — The absolute extreme error

  • Motivation: Focuses on the “worst-case scenario”. It requires that the maximum deviation between the approximating function and the original function at every point in the domain must be as small as possible. Like the vertical distance between the two curves at the widest point in the figure.

2. Mean Square Norm ( norm) — The error of the overall energy

  • Motivation: Focuses on the “overall fitting energy”. It allows for relatively obvious deviations at individual points (such as the Gibbs phenomenon at discontinuities), but requires that the total sum of the squares of the errors over the entire interval (the area) is minimized.

Conclusion: The Fourier series possesses perfect best approximation property in the mean square norm. Geometrically, the truncated Fourier series is precisely the orthogonal projection of the original function onto the finite-dimensional subspace of low frequencies. This geometric essence forms the theoretical foundation for modern functional analysis and modern signal processing.

With the macroscopic intuition regarding “measurements” and “trigonometric basis” from before, the core task of this stage is to rigorously establish the inner product structure of the function space. The Boundary of Convergence: Dirichlet Condition

Writing out the series expression is merely a formal expansion. Under what conditions can this series actually converge, and is its sum strictly equal to the original function ? This requires introducing the Dirichlet condition.

For a function defined on , if the following three conditions are met, its Fourier series is convergent within the interval:

1. Piecewise Continuous

The function has only a finite number of first-kind discontinuities in the interval.

That is, the interval can be divided into a finite number of small subintervals :

such that is continuous in each open subinterval, and the left limit and the right limit exist at the endpoints (they cannot diverge to infinity).

2. Piecewise Monotonic

The function is monotonic in each small interval (either non-increasing or non-decreasing). This means the function has only a finite number of extreme points over the entire large interval, excluding pathological functions that oscillate infinitely densely near the origin, like .

3. Piecewise Differentiable / Bounded Derivative

The function is differentiable in each small interval , and its derivative function is bounded in that interval. This condition further guarantees the local smoothness of the function curve, allowing for perfect convergence at continuous points during series approximation.

When a function satisfies the above Dirichlet conditions, the convergence value of the Fourier series possesses the following extremely beautiful analytical properties:

  • When is a continuous point of , the series converges strictly to the function value:
  • When is a discontinuity point of , the series converges to the arithmetic mean of the left and right limits at that point:

Thus, the Fourier series has moved from the algebraic construction of a space to the rigorous convergence application of analysis.

The Motivation for Best Approximation: A Game Between Data, Physics, and Models

When facing real-world data (Data) from the physical world, we usually want to establish a mathematical model (Model) to describe it. At this point, we face a core contradiction: the trade-off between the model’s complexity (Complexity) and its predictive capability (Prediction).

  • Overfitting: If we relentlessly pursue a perfect fit of the model to the known data points, using extremely complex ultra-high-dimensional functions (such as high-order polynomials or trigonometric series with too many terms), the model will track the noise in the data, leading to violent oscillations. Although the error at the known points is , the predictive capability outside these points will completely collapse.

  • Occam’s Razor: We hope that the model approximates the true data as closely as possible while maintaining a “Simple Model”.

To quantify this “approximation,” we introduce the concept of distance in an inner product space. If the true function is , and the approximating model is , our goal is to minimize the mean square error between them:

In a linear space, the essence of finding this minimum error model is performing an orthogonal projection.

Modern Functional Extension: Sobolev Spaces and Fractional Smoothness

In classical theory, we can only discuss whether integer-order derivatives, such as the first or second, are square-integrable. However, the smoothness of some functions lies precisely between “first derivative square-integrable” and “second derivative square-integrable.” To achieve a more precise quantitative characterization of function smoothness, modern functional analysis introduced the Sobolev Space .

Its core motivation is: To use the weighted sum of Fourier coefficients to completely translate the “differentiation operation in the time domain” into “algebraic weighting in the frequency domain.”
